title: Conjugate roots
steps: Real coefficients make \(3-i\) another root. The roots sum to 10, so the remaining root is \(10-(3+i)-(3-i)=4\).

title: Equation of a sphere
steps: The centre-radius equation is \((x+1)^2+(y-3)^2+z^2=81\). Expanding gives \(x^2+2x+y^2-6y+z^2=71\).

title: Intersecting complex regions
steps: The modulus inequality is the closed disc centred at \((2,3)\) with radius 1. The second condition is \(y\le x\), so retain the small cap below the line \(y=x\), including its boundary.

title: Argument of a quotient
steps: The angle difference is the argument of \(3+4i\), modulo \(2\pi\). Its modulus is 5, so its sine is imaginary part divided by modulus.

title: Negating quantifiers
steps: Change “for every” to “there exists”, change “there exists” to “for every”, and negate the equality. Keep the stated domains of the variables.
answer: C: \(\exists p>0\text{ such that }\forall q>p,\ q^2\ne p\).

title: Partial fractions and primitives
steps: The decomposition is \(\frac1{7(x+1)}-\frac1{7(x-6)}+\frac1{(x-6)^2}\). Its primitive contains two logarithms and a term proportional to \((x-6)^{-1}\).

title: Complex triangle area
steps: At the vertex \(2z-iz\), the two side vectors are \(iz\) and \(-2z\). They are perpendicular, with lengths \(|z|\) and \(2|z|\), so the area is half their product.

title: Comparing vector lines
steps: The second direction vector is \(-2\) times the first. Also \((3,2,-2)=(2,3,-4)+(1,-1,2)\), so the second base point lies on the first line. The lines coincide, hence intersect and are parallel.

title: Counterexample to an inflection claim
steps: For option C, \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)=20x^3+12x^2=4x^2(5x+3)\). This is zero at 0 but positive on both sides sufficiently close to 0, so concavity does not change there.

title: Writing a contrapositive
steps: The contrapositive of “if P then Q” is “if not Q then not P”. For integers, not even means odd.
answer: If a is odd, then a cubed is odd.

title: Adding complex numbers
steps: Collect real and imaginary parts: \(3(3+2i)+(-1-5i)=9-1+(6-5)i\).

title: Angle between unit vectors
steps: Both position vectors have length 1. Their dot product gives \(\cos\theta=1/\sqrt{10}\). Hence \(\tan^2\theta=(1-\cos^2\theta)/\cos^2\theta\).

title: Square roots of a complex number
Product with the conjugate
steps: If \(z=re^{i\theta}\), then \(\bar z=re^{-i\theta}\) and \(|z|=r\). Multiplying gives \(z\bar z=r^2e^{i\theta-i\theta}=r^2\).

title: Completing the square in an integral
steps: At the limits \(x=3\) and \(x=3/2\), the inverse sine values are 0 and \(-\pi/6\).

title: Modulus of a power
steps: \(|z|=a\sqrt2\) since \(a>0\). The modulus of the fifth power is the fifth power of the modulus.

title: Principal argument of a power
steps: \(\arg z=\pi/4\), so an argument of \(z^5\) is \(5\pi/4\). Subtract \(2\pi\) to enter the principal range \((-\pi,\pi]\).

title: Exponential form of a trigonometric identity
steps: Expand the fourth power. Since \((2i)^4=16\), the left side is \(\frac1{16}(e^{4i\theta}-4e^{2i\theta}+6-4e^{-2i\theta}+e^{-4i\theta})\).
Pair conjugate exponentials using the supplied identity: \(e^{4i\theta}+e^{-4i\theta}=2\cos4\theta\) and \(e^{2i\theta}+e^{-2i\theta}=2\cos2\theta\).

title: Integrating a fourth power of sine
steps: Euler’s sine identity identifies the fourth power in part (i) as \(\sin^4\theta\). Integrate the three terms separately, dividing by each inner frequency.

title: Constructing a real polynomial
steps: Include the conjugate zeroes \(1-6i\) and \(3+4i\). The conjugate pairs give \((x-1)^2+36\) and \((x-3)^2+16\).

title: Applying the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality
steps: Apply the given inequality to each factor: \(a+7b\ge2\sqrt{7ab}\), \(b+2c\ge2\sqrt{2bc}\), and \(c+14a\ge2\sqrt{14ac}\).
All factors are positive, so multiplication preserves the inequalities. Their product is at least \(8\sqrt{196a^2b^2c^2}=112abc\).

title: Recovering displacement from acceleration
steps: The graph has period 4 and acceleration amplitude \(\pi^2\), starting at its maximum. Thus \(\ddot x=\pi^2\cos(\pi t/2)\).
Integrating gives \(\dot x=2\pi\sin(\pi t/2)+C_1\). Initial rest gives \(C_1=0\); integrating again gives \(x=-4\cos(\pi t/2)+C_2\). Use \(x(0)=-2\) to obtain \(C_2=2\).

title: Exponential substitution
steps: Put \(u=e^x\), so \(du=e^x\,dx\). The integral becomes \(\int(1+u)/(1+u^2)\,du\).
Split it into \(\int du/(1+u^2)+\int u\,du/(1+u^2)\), then substitute back.

title: Difference of squares pattern
steps: Every positive multiple of 4 is \(4n\) for a positive integer \(n\). The displayed pattern suggests consecutive terms differing by 2: \((n+1)^2-(n-1)^2=4n\).
Both bases are non-negative integers, so this supplies a difference of integer squares for every such multiple.

title: Distance in one oscillation
steps: Complete the square: \(v^2=16-2(x-2)^2\). The turning points occur at \(v=0\), giving \(x=2\pm2\sqrt2\), so the amplitude is \(2\sqrt2\).
One full period traverses four amplitudes, regardless of the starting point.

title: Tangent half-angle substitution
steps: Let \(u=\tan(\theta/2)\). Then \(\cos\theta=(1-u^2)/(1+u^2)\), \(\sin\theta=2u/(1+u^2)\), and \(d\theta=2\,du/(1+u^2)\).
The integral simplifies to \(\int du/(u^2-2u+4)=\int du/((u-1)^2+3)\).
answer: \(\frac1{\sqrt3}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\tan(\theta/2)-1}{\sqrt3}\right)+C\), on each interval where the substitution is continuous.

title: Vertical motion with quadratic resistance
steps: During descent, measure distance \(s\) downwards from the highest point and speed \(v\ge0\). Newton’s law gives \(v\,dv/ds=10-0.1v^2\).

title: Irrationality by contradiction
steps: Suppose \(\sqrt6=p/q\) in lowest positive integer terms. Then \(p^2=6q^2\), so \(p\) is even; write \(p=2r\).
Then \(2r^2=3q^2\), which makes \(q\) even too. This contradicts \(p\) and \(q\) having no common factor.

title: Using a known irrational number
steps: Suppose \(r=\sqrt3-\sqrt2\) is rational. Squaring gives \(r^2=5-2\sqrt6\), hence \(\sqrt6=(5-r^2)/2\) would be rational.
This contradicts part (i).

title: Power failure followed by projectile motion
steps: The squared distance to the transmitter is \((3-t/4)^2+2^2+(t/4)^2\). Setting it to 9 gives \(t^2-12t+32=0\), so the helicopter first enters the 3 m boundary at \(t=4\) s.
At that instant its height is 52 m and its upward velocity is \(1/4\text{ m s}^{-1}\). If \(\tau\) is time after power loss, height is \(52+\tau/4-5\tau^2\).
Setting the height to zero gives \(20\tau^2-\tau-208=0\). The positive root is \((1+129)/40\).

title: Volume by discs and integration by parts
steps: Squaring \(y=x\sqrt{e^x}\) gives \(y^2=x^2e^x\). The disc method gives \(V=\pi\int_0^3x^2e^x\,dx\).
Integrating by parts twice gives the primitive \(e^x(x^2-2x+2)\). Evaluating at 3 and 0 yields \(5e^3-2\).

title: Perpendicular vector condition
steps: With direction vector \(\mathbf d=(6,2,-3)\), use \(\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\mathbf d=0\): \((4-3b,5-4b,2-4b)\cdot(6,2,-3)=28-14b=0\).

title: Two points making a given angle
steps: Now \(B=(6,8,8)\), so \(|AB|=\sqrt{4+9+36}=7\). Triangle ABC is right-angled at A. With angle C equal to \(\pi/4\), it has \(|AC|=|AB|=7\).
The line direction \((6,2,-3)\) also has length 7. Thus the two choices are \(C=A\pm(6,2,-3)\).

title: Separating a velocity equation
steps: The equation of motion used here is \(dv/dt=-(k+v^2)\). Separating and integrating from initial velocity u to velocity v gives \(t=-\int_u^v ds/(k+s^2)\).
Use \(\int ds/(k+s^2)=k^{-1/2}\tan^{-1}(s/\sqrt k)\), since \(k>0\).

title: Testing the direction of motion
steps: Substitute the given time in part (i): \(\tan^{-1}(v/\sqrt k)=\tan^{-1}(u/\sqrt k)-\pi/4\).
Since \(u>0\), the right side lies between \(-\pi/4\) and \(\pi/4\). Therefore \(v<0\) exactly when \(\tan^{-1}(u/\sqrt k)<\pi/4\). Monotonicity of inverse tangent gives \(u<\sqrt k\).
answer: \(0<u<\sqrt k\), using the relation in part (i), with force in the fixed negative direction.

title: Induction for a reciprocal sum
steps: Assume \(S_k>13/24\) for an integer \(k\ge2\). Comparing consecutive sums, \(S_{k+1}-S_k=\frac1{2k+1}+\frac1{2k+2}-\frac1{k+1}=\frac1{(2k+1)(2k+2)}>0\).
Thus \(S_{k+1}>S_k>13/24\), completing the induction.

title: Reflecting a point in a line
steps: The diagram shows \(PM\) perpendicular to the line. Write \(M=A+\lambda(B-A)=(1+\lambda,-1+\lambda,2+\lambda)\), using direction \((1,1,1)\).
Perpendicularity gives \((P-M)\cdot(1,1,1)=0\), so \((3-\lambda)-\lambda+(3-\lambda)=0\). Hence \(\lambda=2\) and \(M=(3,1,4)\).
Because M is the midpoint, \(Q=2M-P\).

title: Length of a complex spiral
steps: The first step runs from \(z_1=8\) to \(z_2=6i\), so its length is \(\sqrt{8^2+6^2}=10\).
Each subsequent difference is multiplied by \(3i/4\), so its length is multiplied by \(3/4\). The total is the convergent geometric sum \(10/(1-3/4)\).

title: A point on a translated unit circle
steps: The radius is 1, so \(z_1-w=\cos(-2\pi/3)+i\sin(-2\pi/3)=-1/2-i\sqrt3/2\). Add \(w=2+i\).

title: Tangency from the origin
steps: Write \(z_2=x+iy\). The circle gives \((x-2)^2+(y-1)^2=1\). A radius is perpendicular to its tangent, so \((x,y)\cdot(x-2,y-1)=0\).
Subtracting these equations gives \(2x+y=4\). Substitution produces \((x-2)(5x-6)=0\). The point shown above and to the left of the centre is \((6/5,8/5)\).
answer: For the point shown, \(z_2=\frac65+\frac85i\). The other tangent point is \(2+0i\).

title: Unit-circle roots from an imaginary part
steps: Put \(z=e^{i\theta}\), with \(0\le\theta<2\pi\). The imaginary-part condition becomes \(\sin3\theta+\sin2\theta+\sin\theta=0\).
Using \(\sin3\theta+\sin\theta=2\sin2\theta\cos\theta\), factor as \(\sin2\theta(2\cos\theta+1)=0\).
The first factor gives \(\theta=0,\pi/2,\pi,3\pi/2\); the second gives \(\theta=2\pi/3,4\pi/3\).

title: Subtracting two related integrals
steps: Combine the integrands over the common denominator: \(\frac1{(1+x^2)^n}-\frac1{(1+x^2)^{n-1}}=\frac{1-(1+x^2)}{(1+x^2)^n}\). Integrating both sides from 0 to 1 gives the required relation.

title: Evaluating a related integral
steps: First, \(I_1=[\tan^{-1}x]_0^1=\pi/4\). To use part (i), differentiate \(x/(1+x^2)\).
Since \(\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x}{1+x^2}=\frac{1-x^2}{(1+x^2)^2}\), its integral is \(I_2+\int_0^1\frac{-x^2}{(1+x^2)^2}\,dx=I_2+(I_2-I_1)\), using part (i).

title: Magnitude of a parametrised circle
steps: Expand the squared norm using the dot product: \(|\mathbf v|^2=\cos^2\theta|\mathbf a|^2+\sin^2\theta|\mathbf b|^2+2\sin\theta\cos\theta(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b)\).
A and B lie on the unit sphere, so their position vectors have length 1; they are perpendicular, so the cross term vanishes.

title: Intersection of two great circles
steps: Every point of \(C_1\) satisfies \(y=2x\), while every point of \(C_2\) satisfies \(z=y\). Thus an intersection has coordinates \((x,2x,2x)\).
Both circles lie on the unit sphere, so \(x^2+4x^2+4x^2=1\), giving \(x=\pm1/3\). Each of these unit vectors lies in both circle planes.

title: Constructing an orthonormal circle basis
steps: Take \(\mathbf a=(0,1,0)\). The projection of \(\overrightarrow{OP}\) onto this unit vector is \((0,1/\sqrt6,0)\). Subtract it to obtain \(\mathbf r=(\sqrt3/2,0,-1/(2\sqrt3))\).
This remainder has length \(\sqrt{5/6}\). Normalising gives \(\mathbf b=(3/\sqrt{10},0,-1/\sqrt{10})\), perpendicular to \(\mathbf a\).
The vectors span the plane through O, A and P. Both are unit vectors, so the supplied circle formula applies; P occurs when \(\cos\theta=1/\sqrt6\) and \(\sin\theta=\sqrt{5/6}\).
